question: What is a synapse, and how does it transfer information?

100 Coordination
Everyday we do many activities such as sharpening of a pencil, grasping
a door knob, walking or running, driving, and a few physical actions.
All
these actions involve well coordinated movements made with well balanced
postures.
In fact, whenever we move some basic functions such as
movement, balance and coordination work together in performing motions
of body parts.
Even standing upright is a challenge of balancing on just two feet with
a narrow base.
Yet, it is common for us not only to stand upright easily and
apparently, effortlessly, but also while keeping our balance to perform
many functions like walking, running etc.
x What other functions do you think are needed in coordination and
balance?
All our functions are carried out by an effort of several systems
working together.
For example, while movement, we hardly ever use just
the skeletal system or muscular system alone, several other systems also
have their own roles to play.
Even within the muscular system, several
muscles work in a systamatic manner.
x What triggers the movement of the muscles?
All our body parts, mainly the tissues and cells in them work by picking
up signals of change (also called as stimuli) from their surroundings.
They
then respond to them.
This process triggers different functions in our body.
For example, it is natural to move to a side of the road when we hear or see
a car approaching.

All living organisms respond to stimuli.
Changes in the surroundings
or signals of changes or stimulus are reasons for responses by living
organisms.
The cat may be running because it saw a mouse.
Plants grow
towards the sunlight.
We start sweating when the surroundings are hot and
humid.
The ability to react to particular stimulus in a particular situation
must be of great importance in ensuring the survival of the organism.
There is a sequence of events that brings about responses.
They start
from detecting a change in outer or inner environment of the body or
stimuli, then transmission of the information is the second stage, processing
of the same is the third stage and execution of the appropriate action is
last stage.

Fig-4: Synapse
Synapse
Synapse is the functional region of contact
between two neurons, where information from one
neuron is transmitted or relayed to another neuron.
Though these are regions of minute gaps and
essentially neurons do not have any protoplasmic
connection between them yet information is passed
from one nerve cell to the other through these gaps
either in the form of chemical or electrical signals
or both.
These synapses are mainly found usually in
the brain, spinal cord and around the spinal cord.
Beyond these areas the axon carries the signals
from brain and spinal cord to respective parts of
our body.
104 Coordination
5.4 Pathways: From stimulus to response
In the holding stick activity you observed that there is coordination
between eye and fingers.
Different pathways are taken by nerves to bring
about this coordinated activity.
On the basis of pathways followed, nerves are classified mainly into
three different types.
They are as follows.
(A) Afferent nerves or Sensory nerves :
The nerves which carry messages towards the central nervous system
(spinal cord or brain) from nerve endings on the muscles of different sense
organs are called afferent or sensory nerves.
(B) Efferent nerves or motor nerves :
The nerves which carry messages from the central nervous system to
body parts that shall carry out the response to effector muscles are called
efferent or motor nerves.
(C) Association nerves (Interneurons) :
These nerves link together the afferent and efferent nerves in central
nervous system (brain and spinal cord).

parsed_output.answer: A synapse is the functional region of contact between two neurons, where information from one neuron is transmitted or relayed to another neuron. The transfer of information across a synapse occurs through either chemical or electrical signals, or both. When an electrical impulse reaches the end of an axon, it triggers the release of chemical messengers called neurotransmitters. These neurotransmitters cross the synapse and bind to receptors on the dendrites of the next neuron, thereby transmitting the signal.
